The Pureau process

How we make Australia's Purest Water

Ordinary tap water goes in. Three filtration stages take out what you don't want, with no treatment chemicals. Then it's independently lab tested, filled into BPA Free 10L casks and sent to your local stockist.

Free of chlorine, bacteria, fluoride and sodium. Lab tested.

First stage

Filtration

Carbon and inorganic media remove chlorine, nitrates, iron and sediment. This conditions the water before the high-pressure membrane step.

Second stage

Reverse osmosis

Water is forced through semi-permeable membranes at high pressure. Fluoride, sodium and dissolved solids are rejected at the membrane.

Third stage

Biological filters

0.2-micron absolute filters remove any remaining bacteria and microbes. Samples go to ALS for independent verification every single production run.

What the Pureau process removes

These are the substances found in Australian tap water and many bottled waters that do not exist in Pureau.

Stage 1
Chlorine
Added to tap water as a disinfectant. Carbon filtration removes it completely.
Stage 1
Nitrates
Common in agricultural catchments. Removed by specialised inorganic media.
Stage 1
Iron and sediment
Dissolved metals and particulate matter from infrastructure and source water.
Stage 1
Stage 2
PFAS
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — "forever chemicals". Removed at two stages: activated carbon filtration, then the reverse osmosis membrane.
Stage 2
Fluoride
State-mandated addition to tap water. Rejected by the reverse osmosis membrane.
Stage 2
Sodium
Dissolved sodium salts present in most Australian tap and spring waters.
Stage 2
Heavy metals
Lead, arsenic, cadmium and chromium. The reverse osmosis membrane rejects dissolved metal ions at 95–99% efficiency.
Stage 3
Bacteria
0.2 micron absolute filtration is the accepted sterilising grade for bacterial removal in food and beverage production.

Independently verified. Every run.

Pureau sends samples to Australian Laboratory Services (ALS) across every production run at our Erskine Park facility. Results are reviewed and signed off before any product leaves the site.

Not all Reverse Osmosis systems are the same

A home filter and a Pureau plant are different things.

Reverse osmosis is just one step in our process. A Reverse Osmosis system alone does not guarantee 100% purity. That's why we independently verify the quality of every production run. The result depends entirely on what surrounds the membrane — and most home systems leave out the parts that matter most.

△

The storage tank problem

Most under-bench and benchtop home Reverse Osmosis units store purified water in a pressurised rubber bladder tank. Still water sitting in a rubber vessel in a warm cabinet is a known environment for bacterial regrowth. By the time it reaches your glass, the purification has been partially reversed.

△

Filter fatigue goes undetected

Home systems depend on the owner replacing pre-filters every 6 to 12 months. An exhausted carbon pre-filter allows chlorine and organic compounds through to the RO membrane, degrading it from the front. Contaminant rejection rates fall quietly, with no alarm and no visible sign.

△

No biological filtration stage

A Reverse Osmosis membrane rejects dissolved solids — it does not filter bacteria. Pureau adds a third stage of biological filtration to 0.2 microns absolute after the membrane. Most home systems stop at the membrane. That gap is where bacteria live.

△

Stage count is not purity

Some home systems are marketed as 7-stage or 9-stage. In most cases the additional stages are mineral-addition cartridges, alkaline stones or UV lamps — each addressing taste or marketing, not purification. More stages does not mean cleaner water.

△

Cold water cuts performance

Reverse Osmosis membrane efficiency drops significantly in cold water — a common condition in Australian winters, particularly in southern states. Rejection rates can fall by 15 to 25 per cent in cold supply water with no indication to the user that the system is underperforming.

△

No independent verification

Pureau sends samples to Australian Laboratory Services (ALS) across every production run. A home Reverse Osmosis system has no ongoing third-party testing. What the membrane claims to remove, and what it actually removes on any given day, are two different things without verified data to confirm it.

The real numbers

What a home Reverse Osmosis actually produces.

NSF/ANSI 58 — the standard most home Reverse Osmosis units are certified to — only requires a unit to demonstrate 75% TDS rejection at test conditions. Real-world performance, with aged membranes and suburban water pressure, falls further. These are established industry and independent research findings.

Home Reverse Osmosis real-world figures reflect typical consumer-grade systems after 12–24 months of use at suburban mains pressure (50–80 PSI). Pureau figures reflect ALS-verified production results.

A home Reverse Osmosis cannot produce Pureau.

The pressure is not high enough. The pre-treatment beds are not there. The biological filtration stage after the membrane does not exist. The storage tank introduces contamination the membrane just removed. And there is no independent laboratory test to tell you any of this is happening.

Pureau operates at industrial membrane pressures home systems cannot physically reach, through carbon and sand pre-treatment banks, through a three-stage process that ends with biological filtration to 0.2 microns absolute — then sealed, not stored in rubber. Every production run is tested independently. Not occasionally. Every run.

Common questions

Frequently asked questions

Where do I get my minerals if Pureau has none?

From food. Dietary minerals come overwhelmingly from what you eat, not what you drink — the mineral content of tap and spring water is incidental rather than nutritionally significant. Pureau's job is hydration. If you want minerals in your water you can add exactly the ones you choose, in the amount you choose, to a known starting point of zero. That isn't possible with any water that already has minerals in it.

What is Pureau?

Pureau is 100% purified water produced through a three-stage industrial process: carbon and sand filtration, high-pressure reverse osmosis, and 0.2-micron biological filtration. It contains no minerals, fluoride, chlorine, sodium or bacteria.

Does Pureau contain fluoride?

No. Australian tap water is fluoridated by state water authorities. The Pureau reverse osmosis process removes fluoride completely. Confirmed by independent ALS laboratory testing across every production run.

Is Pureau tested regularly?

Yes. Pureau sends samples to Australian Laboratory Services (ALS) across every production run. Results are reviewed before any product leaves the facility. Not batch tested. Not sampled. Every run.

How can you be sure there is no contamination during production?

All piping in the Pureau facility is food-grade stainless steel. Every morning, 45 minutes before production begins, the entire system is steam sterilised. No cleaning chemicals are used — steam is the sterilant. The water never touches anything that could reintroduce contamination.

Is Pureau tested for microplastics?

Microplastic testing is not part of the standard ALS production run protocol. The main microplastic risk with any packaged water is the packaging itself, not the source water. Pureau uses an approved supplier programme for all packaging materials. The Bag in Box format uses significantly less plastic contact surface per litre than single-serve bottled formats, and the 0.2-micron biological filtration stage removes any particulates present in the production water before filling.

Why does pure water have a lower pH?

Pureau leaves the facility at pH 7.1–7.4. Without dissolved minerals to act as buffers, the water absorbs a small amount of CO₂ from the air, lowering the pH over time. This is normal chemistry — the same process that occurs with rainwater — and has no health significance.

What formats does Pureau come in?

600 mL bottles (6-pack and 12-pack), 2 L bottles, 5 L Bag in Box casks and 10 L Bag in Box casks. The cask’s inner bag collapses as water is dispensed, keeping the remaining water sealed from air.

Is the packaging recyclable?

The outer carton is fully recyclable kerbside. The inner liner is not currently accepted in kerbside collections — check locally for soft-plastic take-back options in your area. One 10 L cask replaces 17 individual 600 mL plastic bottles.

How long does an open cask last?

Once tapped, use within 30 days and keep out of direct sunlight. The Bag in Box design keeps air out as water is dispensed, so the water stays fresh throughout.

Where is Pureau made?

Pureau is manufactured at the Erskine Park facility in Western Sydney, operated by Australian Beverage Holdings. Australian owned and operated.

Where can I buy Pureau?

Pureau is available at Woolworths, Coles and IGA stores nationally, and online via Woolworths, Coles and Amazon AU for home delivery.
